# Repository concepts

This document owns repository-specific design, lifecycle, and operator decisions that span files. It is not a file inventory or a replacement for the [chezmoi reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/). Source files define behavior; [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) owns contributor workflows and safety boundaries and routes each maintenance task here or to a narrower path rule or skill.

## Bootstrap

Bootstrap remains interactive because it crosses account-specific input, system-level installation, and hardware-backed GPG keys. Scripts provision tools and machine state that file synchronization alone cannot express.

Scripts in [`.chezmoiscripts`](../.chezmoiscripts/) use [chezmoi's script lifecycle](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/use-scripts-to-perform-actions/) rather than a repository-specific runner. Their names have no ordering prefixes, so a script that needs a sibling in the same phase checks for it before writing anything. Once- and change-triggered provisioning deliberately does not act as a health check; repairing a removed tool or a changed card's key requires explicitly rescheduling setup.

For a single `run_onchange` script, use [`chezmoi state delete`](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/commands/state/#delete) with bucket `entryState` and key `$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/<target name>`; the target name omits `run_onchange_before_` or `run_onchange_after_` and `.tmpl`. For example, to reschedule only `run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl`, then review and apply that script:

```sh
chezmoi state delete --bucket=entryState --key="$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/setup-gitconfig.sh"
chezmoi status --exclude=encrypted "$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/setup-gitconfig.sh"
chezmoi diff --recursive --exclude=encrypted "$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/setup-gitconfig.sh"
chezmoi apply "$HOME/.chezmoiscripts/setup-gitconfig.sh"
```

That target key does not reschedule `run_once` scripts. Use [chezmoi's bucket-wide reset procedure](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/use-scripts-to-perform-actions/#clear-the-state-of-all-run_onchange_-and-run_once_-scripts) only when rerunning an entire class is intended: deleting `scriptState` reschedules all `run_once` scripts, and deleting `entryState` reschedules all `run_onchange` scripts, including this repository's YubiKey-dependent GPG setup. Prepare for those scripts' interactive requirements before a full apply.

Treat provisioning comments as operational input: editing them can [reschedule a script](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/use-scripts-to-perform-actions/#understand-how-scripts-work), and a `Brewfile` edit changes the explicit hash embedded in its installer. Edit them only when the resulting rerun is in scope.

Most tools a script runs print progress or no-op notices that only matter when they fail. Run such an external command through `step` from [`.chezmoiscripts/.lib/step.zsh`](../.chezmoiscripts/.lib/step.zsh), which the script sources from `$CHEZMOI_SOURCE_DIR`: it replaces the command's output with a status line naming the command and replays the output only when the command fails, and `chezmoi apply -v` streams the output instead. A command that prints nothing when it has nothing to do needs no wrapper. A wrapped command reads `/dev/null` and by default shows nothing while it runs, so commands that need the user, such as vendor installers, `brew bundle`, sudo, browser sign-in, GUI launches, and YubiKey operations, stay unwrapped. Editing the library changes no script's content, so it reruns nothing and takes effect when each script next runs. Adopting it does change a script's content, so a script whose rerun needs the user adopts it only along with another change to that script.

These dependencies shape the sequence:

- Homebrew and [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile) packages provide tools used by later scripts.
- proto resolves every tool version from `~/.proto/.prototools`, which chezmoi writes from [`dot_proto/dot_prototools`](../dot_proto/dot_prototools) during file synchronization. The dev-tools script runs in the `after` phase so proto can read that declaration before installing runtimes and reconciling the npm, uv, and mbx tools. In the `before` phase that file does not exist yet, and proto refuses to install a tool whose required Node.js version is unconfigured.
- `claude` and `pi` come from their vendor installers in `run_once_after_install-agent-clis.sh`, and `codex` comes from the `codex` cask declared in [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile). The script runs in the `after` phase because Pi needs the Node that `~/.proto/.prototools` declares.
- launchd LaunchAgents own gpg-agent and keyboxd, and `no-autostart` in `~/.gnupg/common.conf` stops every client from starting one implicitly: a daemon started from a sandboxed agent shell keeps that sandbox for life and cannot reach the YubiKey. The GPG script writes and bootstraps those jobs in the `before` phase after Homebrew installation, because chezmoi needs the private keys while synchronizing encrypted files. It is `run_onchange` keyed on the Homebrew kegs those daemons link, so an upgrade of gnupg or of one of its libraries restarts them with the files now on disk. dirmngr is deliberately unmanaged, so keyserver operations fail explicitly instead of autostarting it; the script imports the card's public key over HTTPS from the URL stored on the card instead of using the card's `fetch` command.

A dedicated case-sensitive `Code` volume is provisioned as machine infrastructure rather than managed as a normal file target. It is unique, belongs to the APFS container that stores `$HOME`, and is mounted persistently by UUID through `vifs`. Provisioning must refuse to mount over a non-empty `~/Code` or to proceed when `~/Code` or the volume is mounted elsewhere, and must never unmount a volume automatically; a matching volume already mounted at `~/Code` is reused whatever it holds. The `run_once` script provisions fresh-machine state rather than reconciling later drift; its Python test covers deterministic logic, while APFS, Disk Arbitration, and reboot acceptance remain manual Mac checks.

## Package and tool ownership

Where a tool is declared follows from how much update lag its owner tolerates:

- Coding agents tolerate none. `claude` and `pi` come from their vendor installers, unpinned, in one `run_once` script in the `after` phase; `claude` updates itself, while `pi` updates only when `pi update` runs, so the unattended-upgrades job invokes it. Pi keeps its managed install rather than its Homebrew formula or npm package because only the managed install pins its transitive dependencies. `codex` comes from the official `homebrew/cask` CLI cask in [`Brewfile`](../Brewfile), which moves its update onto the same job and reports `brew upgrade --cask codex` as its update action.
- Agent-adjacent CLIs (`ctx7`, `oracle`) also sit in `Brewfile`; `oracle` comes from `steipete/tap` because it has no self-updater. `brew bundle` has no entry type for gh extensions, so [`run_onchange_after_install-gh-extensions.sh`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_install-gh-extensions.sh) installs `gh stack` and `gh actions-lock` at apply time, which needs no gh sign-in: Claude Code's sandbox cannot write gh's extension directory, so an agent there cannot install them on first use.
- Background development tools (`typescript`, `typescript-language-server`, Pyright, mbx) are pinned in `.github/dev-tools` and bumped by Renovate behind a release-age window.
- Runtimes (`node`, `bun`, `pnpm`, `go` through proto; Rust through rustup) resolve through their own managers, with no pin and no window. The `oracle` and `ctx7` formulae pull in Homebrew's `node` (and `pnpm` for oracle), which sits behind proto's shims on `PATH` and is not a runtime channel, so those CLIs execute a Node this repository does not pin.
- GUI and daily-use apps are `Brewfile` casks, and App Store-only apps are `mas` entries. Logseq deliberately remains outside Homebrew ownership: this machine uses manually installed 0.10.15 because 2.x is incompatible, so its cask is not a fallback path.

The Brewfile installer uses [`brew bundle --no-upgrade`](https://docs.brew.sh/Manpage#bundle-subcommand) to separate provisioning from upgrades. The unattended-upgrades job below owns formula and cask upgrades; App Store update preferences remain machine-local.

The managed [LaunchAgent](../private_Library/private_LaunchAgents/com.liby.unattended-upgrades.plist.tmpl) declares the background upgrade schedule and intentionally adds an immediate login or reload run. Its [helper](../private_Library/private_Application%20Support/com.liby.unattended-upgrades/executable_unattended-upgrades) has its own executable path so Login Items can name the job after its basename. The [registration script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-unattended-upgrades.sh.tmpl) embeds both files' hashes so changing either reloads the job after file synchronization; a `Brewfile` change never reloads it.

The helper coordinates Homebrew with Pi, extension, and Rust updates, periodic package-cache cleanup, and post-upgrade maintenance. Both it and the Brewfile installer clear quarantine from the Codex cask's executables, because approving the CLI alone does not cover its helpers or their replacements. The helper also restarts missing or outdated GnuPG daemons; a library-only upgrade needs the next `chezmoi apply` because the reported GnuPG version does not change. These responsibilities require one job beyond Homebrew's package upgrades; the helper owns its command sequence and PATH.

Apps with their own updater stay outside the job's upgrade policy: [`dot_homebrew/brew.env`](../dot_homebrew/brew.env) selects Homebrew's [`HOMEBREW_NO_UPGRADE_AUTO_UPDATES_CASKS`](https://docs.brew.sh/Manpage#environment), using cask declarations rather than a second repository list. Keep `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` unset while that file lives at `~/.homebrew/brew.env`, and keep `--greedy` out of the background job to preserve the boundary. Casks without `auto_updates`, such as `codex`, remain job-owned.

The exact global npm tool versions live in [`.github/dev-tools/package.json`](dev-tools/package.json), Pyright lives in [`.github/dev-tools/requirements.txt`](dev-tools/requirements.txt), and mbx is pinned in [its release installer](dev-tools/install-mbx.sh), which checks the official release archive against the release's `SHA256SUMS` and installs it into `~/.local/bin`. Renovate groups these declarations with other dependencies, and one shared `run_onchange` installer installs the proto-declared tools and then reconciles each declaration independently without pruning unrelated machine-local tools; do not split the installer. The dev-tools workflow supplies their status check; a file-scoped Renovate `ignoreTests` must not be restored because it can become branch-level configuration on a mixed dependency group. `typescript`, `typescript-language-server`, and Pyright back Claude Code's LSP plugins, which [`.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json`](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) enables; `typescript-language-server` falls back to the global `typescript` when a workspace's own cannot provide tsserver.

Each of these declarations carries a release-age cooldown, so a compromised upstream release has time to be reported and yanked before it is pinned here. npm and PyPI enforce it twice, and the two halves are coupled: the installer refuses to resolve an artifact younger than its window, so the matching Renovate rule in [`.github/renovate.json`](renovate.json) has to wait at least as long or it pins a version the installer cannot reach. [`dot_config/uv/uv.toml`](../dot_config/uv/uv.toml) sets the PyPI window through uv's `exclude-newer`, and the installer renders the same value into its own `uv tool install` command rather than relying on uv discovering the deployed file. The installer sets the npm window through `npm config set`, which writes it to `~/.npmrc`; an environment variable set in `.zshenv` would miss npm processes that do not inherit that environment. `~/.npmrc` also carries registry tokens, so the source declares the setting through the command rather than tracking the file. The GitHub release rule is mbx's only window, because its installer fetches the exact pinned release. All windows are the same value, and one value is enough because the declarations hold only background tools that nobody waits on.

`Brewfile` owns the `proto` executable; upgrade it through Homebrew only. Proto's [self-upgrade command](https://moonrepo.dev/docs/proto/commands/upgrade) installs a copy under `$PROTO_HOME/bin`, which shadows Homebrew in this repository's toolchain PATH. [`dot_proto/dot_prototools`](../dot_proto/dot_prototools) deliberately selects [version aliases](https://moonrepo.dev/docs/proto/commands/install#installing-one-tool), including [Node's LTS selection](https://moonrepo.dev/docs/proto/commands/pin), and enables proto's [automatic installation and cleanup](https://moonrepo.dev/docs/proto/config#settings); this setup accepts runtime version movement without a release-age window. Proto's standalone installer is not a fallback path.

mbx is the machine's Cargo build cache. [`dot_zshenv`](../dot_zshenv) places its Cargo shim ahead of `~/.cargo/bin`, so projects and agents need no separate mbx steps. Keep rustup's default on stable and pin a dated nightly in projects that need one: the background job would advance a bare nightly daily and invalidate that toolchain's cached outputs. The dev-tools installer puts the store at `~/Code/.mbx`, on the same APFS volume as the checkouts for cheap moves and clones. Keep Cargo's default target location so those outputs participate in [mbx's managed-target lifecycle](https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/managed-targets).

Changing mbx's [cache directory](https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/configuration) on an existing machine requires explicit migration of the old store; changing the setting alone leaves the old data outside collection. For suspect build outputs, run [mbx verification](https://mr-boxington.jdx.dev/troubleshooting) with `MBX_VERIFY=1` in a fresh target directory so Cargo actually compiles the units being checked.

[`.chezmoiexternal.toml`](../.chezmoiexternal.toml) pins the zsh plugin archives at fixed commits. The GitHub archive manager in [`.github/renovate.json`](renovate.json) updates those commits from each declared branch.

## Repository validation

GitHub discovers workflow YAML only directly under [`.github/workflows`](workflows/), so keep that directory flat. Checks cheap and deterministic enough to run on every change are jobs in the unfiltered [`validate-repository`](workflows/validate-repository.yml) workflow; a check gets its own path-filtered file only when it is slow or depends on the network. Keep behavior tests beside their owner when chezmoi ignores the test filename; reserve [`.github/tests`](tests/) for repository-only tests that cannot safely live beside a managed source. Bun tests there use the `*.test.ts` name and run through `bun test ./.github/tests/`; Python tests use the conventional `test_*.py` name that `unittest discover` finds there; add a concern subdirectory only when multiple tests benefit from that grouping.

A check derives its expectation from the source that owns the contract, such as a parsed configuration, an include list, frontmatter, or the list a script itself declares, or it states a requirement that source must meet, such as the tools a hook must cover. Do not copy a file's current values, wording, or command help into a test as its expected value: such a test fails on behavior-preserving edits and protects nothing the copied file does not already state. Add a check only for a realistic edit whose failure would otherwise surface after it is merged and applied, or never, such as an automerged Renovate pin or a hook that stops running; a removed flag or a missing credential that the next call reports needs none. The repository deliberately leaves these unvalidated:

- Installed CLI behavior. Homebrew upgrades the CLIs that skills call several times a day, independently of this repository, so a check that runs when a skill changes runs at the wrong time. Verify a skill's CLI syntax against the installed version when editing it; an adopted skill follows the upstream tag recorded in its `metadata`.
- Runtime enforcement of skill frontmatter. The [skill registry test](../dot_agents/skills/skills.test.ts) checks each skill's frontmatter against the rules Claude Code, Codex, and Pi apply when loading it, including that every key is one Claude Code documents; whether a runtime honors a field's value, such as Claude Code's auto mode dropping interpreter grants from `allowed-tools`, needs a check in that runtime. Codex's skill catalog budget counts every installed skill, not only this repository's; past it, Codex shortens every listed description, user skills included, without a warning.
- Credential-path policy for tool calls, which the [agent guard](#agent-guard) package owns and tests. The guard cannot see the file bodies a diff prints, so the review skill's own instruction keeps changed secret-bearing files out of its diffs.
- The content of instruction and documentation prose, such as which routes `AGENTS.md` lists or whether text restated for another reader, like the auto-mode scope entry, still matches its source. A test cannot tell a deliberate rewrite or removal from a mistake, so the diff review owns it.
- Template rendering. The scoped `chezmoi diff` before each commit renders every changed target on the machine that applies it, so a CI render would need its own synthetic data and catch nothing that diff misses.
- Anything that needs the Keychain, the YubiKey, a signed-in account, or a fresh machine, such as `guard-bash` running before Homebrew has installed the guard; those stay manual checks on the Mac.

Every path-filtered workflow lists itself, the tests or validator it runs, and the production sources that can change the result. When a non-required workflow filters both `pull_request` and `push`, use a [YAML anchor](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations#yaml-anchors-and-aliases) for the identical path lists. GitHub leaves the required check for a [workflow skipped by pull-request path filters](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks#handling-skipped-but-required-checks) pending, so before making one required, trigger it for every pull request and move any filtering below the workflow level. Reference each action by its version tag and let [`actions.lock`](workflows/actions.lock) lock it to a commit: run `gh actions-lock` after adding a workflow or changing a `uses` reference, since GitHub enforces the lockfile only for the workflows it lists. Renovate regenerates the lockfile with its own action updates, so its configuration pins no digests, which the lockfile would replace again. Keep `permissions` read-only, disable checkout credential persistence, cancel superseded runs for the same ref, and give every job a finite timeout. Extract a reusable workflow only for a complete job shared by multiple callers, or a composite action for a meaningful repeated step sequence; do not hide isolated fields or one checkout step behind an abstraction.

The `validate-repository` workflow runs for every pull request and every push to `main`, so its checks have no path list that a rename can leave stale, and it can become required without a path-filter skip deadlock.

## Configuration ownership

Most source files and templates render to paths under `$HOME`. Standard source names and template mechanics follow chezmoi rather than repository-specific conventions.

Not every configuration is fully replaced. Applications such as Codex and Claude Code write mutable runtime state, so [`modify_` sources](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/target-types/#modify-file) manage selected fields while preserving application-owned values.

Replace subtrees that source fully owns so that removed fields disappear from the destination. For shared subtrees, preserve application-owned fields through an overlay or explicit exceptions during replacement. Establish ownership from the application's writers rather than the shape of the configuration. An overlay preserves undeclared fields; removing a source declaration does not by itself retire its destination state.

The repository requires explicit cleanup of retired paths instead of [chezmoi removal lists](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/special-files/chezmoiremove/), so source describes current configuration without accumulating past removals. Review both obsolete files and retired fields in shared configurations when updating an existing machine; an empty `chezmoi status` is not that review.

The JSON and TOML modifiers emit their input unchanged when its parsed values already match, so neither an application's own formatting nor the key order in a fragment registers as drift. Fragments embedded in scripts, such as [`codex/requirements.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml), also affect script trigger hashes; their ordering changes can rerun the consuming script.

chezmoi source manages portable, durable preferences, including established interaction habits, when they should remain consistent across machines. It leaves matching convenience defaults implicit unless an explicit value enforces a repository boundary or counters observed write-back drift. Generated runtime state, machine-specific paths, and settings synchronized elsewhere remain owned by their existing systems.

The [macOS defaults script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-macos-defaults.sh.tmpl) owns the Apple UI preferences. Its whole-array writes replace a list wholesale, so a tile dragged into the Dock, a stack, or an input source added by hand does not survive a rerun, and its input source, language, and appearance values take effect at the next login rather than in the running session. Each key's own reason stays in that script's adjacent comment. The [app setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-apps.sh) owns the third-party app preferences written with `defaults`, with each key's reason likewise in its adjacent comment, and registers login items through System Events, which writes the database the Login Items pane shows rather than a preference domain. A single fixed archived value, such as Xnip's shortcut, is written by that script as data; an app that stores many archived values and offers a readable export, such as Input Source Pro, is imported from [that export](../.chezmoitemplates/input-source-pro/settings.json) instead, by [a script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_import-input-source-pro.sh.tmpl) that runs when the export changes and replaces the app's settings without the confirmation its own import dialog asks for.

Rex has [a separate preference and reload lifecycle](#rex-integration) because quitting it during an apply would terminate the pane running that apply.

The [notification script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_after_setup-macos-notifications.py) owns selected per-app preferences in usernoted's records, where preferences and notification registration data share the same store. That store sits in usernoted's group container, which macOS opens only to a terminal whose hosting app has Full Disk Access, so without that grant apply stops there. Reload intent persists between applies because matching stored preferences alone do not prove that usernoted has adopted them. The flag layout is private to macOS and must be revalidated against System Settings when changing supported major versions.

Updating selected fields still requires writing the whole `apps` array. A notification registration or preference changed between reading and writing can be overwritten, including for an app outside the selected policy; this window is an accepted trade-off of automatic synchronization. Reloading usernoted may dismiss visible banners.

### Shell startup

Exports needed by agents and chezmoi scripts, and toolchain directories that must precede Homebrew, belong in [`~/.zshenv`](../dot_zshenv) so they do not depend on interactive startup or an agent's shell snapshot. Keep that division aligned with [zsh's startup-file contract](https://zsh.sourceforge.io/Doc/Release/Files.html#Startup_002fShutdown-Files). Homebrew's and OrbStack's environment belong in [`~/.zprofile`](../dot_zprofile), which restores toolchain precedence after macOS's `path_helper`. [`~/.zshrc`](../dot_zshrc) holds interactive configuration: completion, history, aliases, plugins, proto activation, and the prompt. Pi's `bash -c` and the launchd helper instead need an inherited or explicitly set PATH; neither consumes these zsh files.

### Codex configuration

[`.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml) declares the source-owned portion of [Codex's user configuration](https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-reference/). The [modifier](../dot_codex/modify_private_config.toml) replaces `plugins`, `permissions.development`, and each source-declared `mcp_servers` table, carrying forward only the destination's existing `node_repl.env` and `node_repl.env_vars` within those server tables. All other declared configuration is deep-overlaid. Replacing server tables removes stale transport fields that can make Codex reject the whole configuration. Removing an entire server from source still requires explicit destination cleanup. While `default_permissions` is set, every apply also deletes `sandbox_mode` and `sandbox_workspace_write`, because those legacy selectors can override the profile.

Leave `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, and per-app authorization out of source (its `apps.*` tables declare only each app's `enabled` flag) so changes made in Desktop, the TUI, or the live file survive an apply.

Desktop generates `node_repl` environment fields and can later replace its runtime tables, so an apply does not prevent subsequent application write-backs. Do not declare the legacy standalone `mcp_servers.computer-use` registration in source: source declarations can override the same-named plugin registration and conflict with [Desktop-owned runtime state](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/24387#issuecomment-4531286877).

Keep the bundled `computer-use` and `unified-computer-use` plugins enabled; `unified-computer-use` provides Desktop's `cua_repl` browser and computer runtime. Keep the bundled `code-review` plugin disabled: it adds a second GitHub path for pull-request comments and merges beside the `gh` and `review` skills.

Desktop persists registered preferences under `[desktop]` and removes their legacy global-state or persisted-atom copies after migration. Manage a registered preference in [`.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/config.toml); reserve the global-state fragment for current persisted atoms that have no registered Desktop setting.

`~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json` is also partially managed. Its [modifier](../dot_codex/modify_dot_codex-global-state.json) overlays [the portable preferences declared by the fragment](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/global-state.json) and leaves every other entry Desktop-owned. These keys belong to the current Desktop implementation rather than the public `config.toml` schema, so verify the installed app before changing or expanding their managed paths. A running Desktop process can overwrite an external apply with its in-memory persisted-atom values, so change these preferences through the UI or apply this target while Desktop is stopped.

Keep `approval_policy = "on-request"`, `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"`, and the sole custom `default_permissions = "development"` profile together. [`.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml`](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml) constrains that tuple because Desktop builds a new task's approval policy and reviewer from its saved agent mode rather than from `config.toml` ([#33552](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/33552)): unconstrained, the saved `auto` mode yields `on-request` / `user` and `full-access` yields `never` / `user`. The constraint intentionally removes the built-in modes, including Full Access. Restart Desktop after changing that file: no reproduction has yet shown Desktop hot-reloading an edited `requirements.toml`.

The same requirements file registers managed hooks from `~/.codex/managed-hooks`: [`guard-bash`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_guard-bash) as the one `PreToolUse` Bash hook, which hands each event to the shared [agent guard](#agent-guard), and [`contextual-markdown-links`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_contextual-markdown-links) on `UserPromptSubmit`, which adds the Markdown link-placement instruction to every prompt.

The [Codex requirements script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-codex-requirements.sh.tmpl) installs the rendered requirements as root-owned `/etc/codex/requirements.toml` and needs sudo, so apply it from an interactive terminal.

The `development` filesystem profile remains standalone with `:root = write`, `~/.ssh` denied except the exact `config`, `allowed_signers`, and `known_hosts` entries that ssh and Git signature verification use, exact read-only `.env` and `.env.local` entries under every workspace root, and no copied per-tool cache lists or broad command allows. Programs may consume credential and environment files through their normal interfaces; changing or deleting one still requires the user's explicit request. Filesystem capability does not authorize remote Git or secret-bearing chezmoi operations.

The [Browser modifier](../dot_codex/browser/modify_config.toml) overlays [its template](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/browser/config.toml) on the full-CDP and upload allowlists Desktop writes to that file; the template deliberately overrides that posture for the Browser tool, granting no-prompt full-CDP control so an agent run is not gated on a human at the keyboard.

[openai/codex#40254](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/40254) tracks the current macOS reproduction in which Chrome fails trusted RPC path validation without an explicit Browser cache read rule. Keep `~/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled/browser` as the only extra read-only path so the trusted worker can load Desktop's runtime-owned Browser service; a chezmoi `private_` or `readonly_` source and `chmod` do not create a trusted permission root. Remove the exception only after deleting the source rule, applying the rendered configuration, fully restarting Desktop, confirming the effective permission table no longer contains the rule, and succeeding on the first Chrome initialization in a fresh task without a prior Browser attempt or retry.

`features.network_proxy = true` enforces the `development` profile's domain and Unix socket rules for sandboxed commands. Claude Code and Codex render their shared domains and Unix socket paths from [`sandbox/allowed-domains.json`](../.chezmoitemplates/sandbox/allowed-domains.json) and [`sandbox/allowed-unix-sockets.json`](../.chezmoitemplates/sandbox/allowed-unix-sockets.json). `allow_local_binding` lets commands listen on local ports and reach loopback directly, as development servers and browser SSO callbacks need. It also turns off the proxy's private-address check: an allowlisted hostname that resolves to a private address is admitted, an unlisted private or link-local address such as a cloud metadata endpoint is refused only as off the allowlist, and Codex puts the private ranges in `NO_PROXY`, so a direct connection to a LAN address fails in the OS sandbox as a connection error rather than a policy denial. The socket entries permit GnuPG, OrbStack's Docker daemon, Rex, the ra broker, Maskey's Keychain service, and the `~/.cache/codex-tmp` directory that Codex sets as commands' `TMPDIR`, where tools bind their own sockets. Web search, MCP, Browser, and Computer Use have separate network controls. Restart Desktop after changing the proxy feature so commands use the updated policy.

The proxy ends the whole command at its first denied request and reports `Network access to "<host>" was blocked: <reason>`, while Claude Code's sandbox only lists the denial in `<sandbox_violations>` and lets the command continue. A host that Claude Code reports beside a command's real work therefore also fails that command under Codex. When a tool sends such a request on its own, as telemetry, an update check, or a platform probe, turn it off with the tool's switch in [`dot_zshenv`](../dot_zshenv), which every zsh reads, terminals and both agents' commands included. Only a request with no switch that zsh startup can set is a candidate for the shared allowlist under its [admission rules](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md#sandbox), and a switch stays set when its host is allowed for another request.

Both `cli_auth_credentials_store` and `mcp_oauth_credentials_store` stay on explicit `keyring`; `auto` may fall back to plaintext files. Before activating this on another machine, use a credential-safe status check against the exact store to confirm the existing login. Agents never migrate, rewrite, or delete the real store.

`features.daemon_auto_start = false` keeps Codex from starting a shared app-server daemon, so each TUI runs its own embedded app server. A shared daemon runs every attached session's hooks and tool commands with the environment of the terminal that first started it, so the [Rex hook](#rex-integration) reports the wrong pane or none, and `REX_*` inside tool commands names a pane the agent is not in ([openai/codex#48500](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/48500)). A TUI still attaches to a daemon that is already running, such as one started before the setting was applied, and stopping that daemon leaves its TUIs offline rather than moving them to embedded servers. To retire it, wait until none of its sessions is working, quit each attached TUI and keep the `codex resume <id>` it prints, run `codex app-server daemon stop`, and resume each session in the pane it came from. `codex queue` does not need the daemon and still reaches a busy embedded session.

### GitLab CLI configuration

glab reads its configuration from `~/.config/glab-cli`, which [`dot_zshenv`](../dot_zshenv) selects with `GLAB_CONFIG_DIR` instead of the macOS default under `~/Library/Application Support`, because Claude Code's sandbox can write `~/.config` but not `~/Library`. glab writes its sign-in state into that `config.yml`, so the [config modifier](../dot_config/private_glab-cli/modify_private_config.yml) sets only the top-level preferences in its [template](../.chezmoitemplates/glab/config.yml), on every apply, and leaves the rest to glab. The [glab setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-glab.sh.tmpl) copies the private host's OAuth application ID from envchain with `glab config set` and runs glab's web sign-in only when glab has never signed in to that host.

Sign-in stores the tokens in that `config.yml` in plaintext instead of glab's default Keychain storage. glab must save new tokens at every refresh and refuses to refresh where it cannot, and Codex cannot run glab where the Keychain is writable: its sandbox denies the shared-memory write that a Keychain write makes, and while its profile denies `~/.ssh`, escalation cannot move a command out of that sandbox. Keychain storage would therefore cost the `~/.ssh` protection, yet it never kept the tokens from agents, which read them through glab inside their sandboxes; what plaintext gives up is the protection of copies of the file, such as backups. Each refresh invalidates the previous tokens, so a copy is useful only until the next refresh, unless a thief refreshes first and keeps the session; glab's next refresh then fails with `invalid_grant`. Sign in again with the setup script's login line: the bare `glab auth login` that `glab auth status` suggests puts the tokens back in the Keychain.

### Claude Code configuration

[`.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md) is the path-scoped owner for Claude Code settings, sandbox, integration, and runtime-state decisions. Its path frontmatter makes Claude Code load it only for the matching sources; other Agents must follow the route in [`AGENTS.md`](../AGENTS.md) before changing those sources.

### Pi configuration

`~/.pi/agent/models.json` and `~/.pi/agent/keybindings.json` are fully managed, while `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` is partially managed. The [settings modifier](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/modify_private_settings.json) replaces each top-level key declared in the [settings fragment](../.chezmoitemplates/pi/settings.json), including the entire `modelThinkingLevels` map, and preserves undeclared keys. Applies intentionally overwrite UI-saved startup and per-model defaults so devices share the source configuration.

Temporary `/model` and `/thinking` selections remain available. After applying settings, use `/reload`, then select the model again with `/model` to activate the thinking defaults; resuming a session can restore its recorded model and thinking level. `defaultProjectTrust = "always"` intentionally lets every directory load project-local settings, resources, packages, and extensions without a trust prompt.

The repository restricts Pi's [`enabledModels`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/settings.md#model-and-thinking) to `rc-gateway/**` and the `anthropic` models in `modelOverrides`, rather than exposing the whole built-in catalog. [The shared model overrides](../.chezmoitemplates/pi/model-overrides.json) supply both Anthropic's `modelOverrides` and the `anthropic/` entries in `enabledModels`. Start a new session (`/new` or a new `pi` process) after changing this scope; `/reload` alone does not activate it. Keep `**` in the gateway pattern because its model IDs include a `vendor/model` slash.

The settings enable Pi's built-in codemode for classifier work. The TypeSafe provider entry overrides only authentication, preserving Pi's built-in classifier catalog and System One protocol adapter.

For `rc-gateway`, derive [`thinkingLevelMap`](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/models-configuration.md) from the entry with the same id under `vercel` in the [models.dev catalog](https://models.dev/api.json). This route fronts Vercel AI Gateway, whose [reasoning mappings](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/models-and-providers/reasoning#how-reasoning-is-mapped) make a successful response insufficient evidence that the requested effort was honored. Map each listed `effort` to the Pi level of the same name and `none` to `off`; encode unsupported levels according to Pi's map definition. Do not alias levels, and keep preferred defaults in `settings.json`.

`contextWindow` in [`private_models.json.tmpl`](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_models.json.tmpl) is this repository's working budget, within what the route accepts. Default to 400000 so sessions compact before long-context quality degrades. When changing a model's budget, recheck its reserve against [Pi's compaction rules](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/docs/compaction.md): keep the working window well above `compaction.reserveTokens` or give the model a `compaction.modelOverrides["provider/modelId"]` entry.

Set `maxTokens` to the smallest of the working window, the vendor's exact documented output limit, and any cap the route actually enforces. A catalog's advertised limit alone is insufficient evidence of a route-enforced cap. Use the working window when the vendor documents no output limit. Check the rendered window and output limit with `pi --list-models rc-gateway`; validate the reasoning map separately.

The [Pi extensions package](https://github.com/Entwining/pi-extensions) owns the editor, footer, guard adapter, and reasoning workaround, including their tests and releases. The [compaction reminder](#shared-agent-instructions) extension stays in this repository because it renders the shared reminder text. [`run_onchange_after_install-pi-extensions.sh`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_install-pi-extensions.sh) installs that Git package after the CLI installer and leaves package registration to Pi, preserving other installed packages and their resource filters.

Pi's `npmCommand` uses npm's [release-age exemption](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/using-npm/config/#min-release-age-exclude) for the whole `@earendil-works/*` scope because Pi pins sibling packages from the same release. Keep the exemption at scope level so those dependencies can update together while third-party packages retain the machine's release-age window. The extensions package checks its development pins with the same window and exemption because Git package installation resolves them too.

Credentials, sessions, installed packages, and recorded trust decisions under `~/.pi/agent` remain runtime-owned, so the directory must never be adopted wholesale. Both managed source directories stay `private_` to preserve mode `0700`. The gateway base URL comes from `.private.rcGatewayBaseUrl`; the rendered model file uses credential commands with the namespaces defined by the [credential consumer contract](#credential-backed-features), rather than carrying secrets.

### Oracle configuration

The [config modifier](../private_dot_oracle/modify_private_config.json) overlays the keys in its [template](../.chezmoitemplates/oracle/config.json) onto `~/.oracle/config.json` and leaves the rest to each machine. `browser.chatgptUrl` stays machine-local because this repository is public. The fragment gives hand-run Oracle the same attach, approval-wait, and model-selection choices as the [oracle skill](../dot_agents/skills/oracle/SKILL.md). It also keeps Chrome in the background and notifications off because the agent starting a run waits for its result.

## Rex integration

With exactly one local Rex app open, run [`setup-rex`](../dot_local/bin/executable_setup-rex) once to import the pinned theme, install Rex's skill, and run [rexume's installer](https://github.com/Entwining/rexume). Run it outside the sandbox from an ordinary Rex pane: the installer writes `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and its daemon keeps that shell's PATH to find `codex` for notices. After changing the theme, run `rexume install` again with the new foreground and background colors.

The [preference script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-rex.sh) writes portable Rex settings without quitting the app that usually hosts the apply; reopen the app to activate them. A separate [reload script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_reload-rex-config.sh.tmpl) reloads the server when the [Lua configuration](../dot_config/rex/init.lua) changes. Remote Control stays on so setup and agent actions work; this adds no reach beyond the server's existing command execution. Themes and session state remain app-owned.

Source owns the Rex and rexume `SessionStart` entries in [Claude's settings fragment](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) and the whole of [Codex's hooks file](../dot_codex/hooks.json). Keep the commands verbatim so `rex skill setup` and `rexume install` recognize them and leave them unchanged. The Pi extension and LaunchAgent belong to rexume's installer and stay out of source. On a new machine, trust the Codex hooks through `/hooks`; keep rexume's entry after Rex's because inserting ahead of a trusted entry makes Codex ask again.

Rex's Integrations settings own its installed skill, but their switches also edit hooks that the next apply restores. Turning off **Integrate with available agents** leaves restored hooks without the skill; turning off **Let agents name sessions** leaves restored hooks requesting names. To keep either switch off, change both source hook entries too.

This repository's orchestration skill is [`orc`](../dot_agents/skills/orc/SKILL.md) to avoid a name conflict with Rex's own skill. It requires rexume tasks and loads Rex's installed guide through `rex skill show`, carrying only this setup's constraints and corrections to that guide. This explicit dependency is intentional under [the skill independence rule](../AGENTS.md#workflow). Keep launch and trust prerequisites inline in `SKILL.md` because reference content is not reliably restored after compaction.

The hook reports the `REX_*` that the process running it inherited, and `rex whoami` accepts any pane that still exists, so those variables must come from the agent's own pane. [Codex configuration](#codex-configuration) therefore keeps Codex TUIs off a shared app-server daemon. An app launched from a Rex pane likewise keeps the pane's `REX_*` and passes them to the terminals and agents it starts, so [`~/.local/bin/open`](../dot_local/bin/executable_open) launches apps from a pane with a Dock launch's environment.

The [apply-time version check](../.chezmoiscripts/run_after_check-skill-versions.sh.tmpl) compares the installed guide and hook state with the Rex version and guide hash in `orc` metadata. An older server requires an update or restart before reviewing drift: the `rex` on PATH belongs to the running server, which can lag behind the updated app.

For a guide warning, read the reported diff, or `rex skill show` when the old guide is not cached, and the Rex changelog since the recorded version. Retest each behavior where `orc` corrects the guide, drop corrections the guide now covers, revise contradictions, and record the new version and hash. For a hook warning, run `rex skill setup` with HOME set to an empty temporary directory and copy its generated entry into the source registrations.

## Agent guard

[`Brewfile`](../Brewfile) installs the [agent-guard package](https://github.com/Entwining/agent-guard) from `Entwining/tap`, providing `/opt/homebrew/bin/agent-guard`. The [Claude Code settings](../.chezmoitemplates/claude/settings.json) register that executable for Bash and file tools. [Codex requirements](../.chezmoitemplates/codex/requirements.toml) keep the hook under `managed_dir`; [`guard-bash`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_guard-bash) checks the Homebrew binary and execs it with `--runtime codex`. The guard adapter in the [Pi extensions package](https://github.com/Entwining/pi-extensions#extensions) maps Pi's tool calls to guard events and invokes the same executable.

The guard reports its own failures, including overrunning its internal deadline, as exit 2, which every runtime treats as a block. A guard that cannot start or a hook that outlives its timeout is up to the runtime: the Pi extension blocks any result other than a clean pass, and the Claude hooks set `onFailure: "block"` because Claude Code would otherwise run the call. Codex runs the call in those cases and has no such setting, so `guard-bash` blocks a missing binary itself and its hook timeout must stay above the guard's deadline.

The package owns guard rules, parser, and tests. This repository owns [`dot_ignore`](../dot_ignore): its `/Library/` entry keeps broad searches above that tree from enumerating it.

## Shared agent instructions

Global behavior shared by Claude Code, Codex, and Pi lives in the ordered section fragments under [`.chezmoitemplates/agents/`](../.chezmoitemplates/agents/). Each fragment owns its section heading, and every root includes each fragment once in the same order. Only the Claude root may append runtime-specific paragraphs; the Codex and Pi roots are assembled from the fragments alone, which the agent-instruction contract test enforces. Do not put a shared heading in a root or copy a shared paragraph there. Keep coding principles in their own fragment so evaluation can remove that rendered section without changing the remaining bytes. Rendered evaluation documents are derived evidence and do not belong in this repository.

Pi consumes the shared core through [`~/.pi/agent/AGENTS.md`](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_AGENTS.md.tmpl), not `APPEND_SYSTEM.md`. The file's `private_` source attribute keeps the rendered instruction file owner-readable only, matching the already-private agent directory. A project `.pi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md` replaces the global file of the same name, while global and project context files coexist in Pi's project context; using the context-file path preserves the global core when a project adds its own instructions.

The runtime adapters deliver [the compaction reminder](../.chezmoitemplates/agents/compaction-reminder.md) to the executor after compaction. The shared evidence rule owns checking carried-forward state, and the [Tools section](../.chezmoitemplates/agents/tools.md) owns restoring skill instructions before their governed actions; the reminder routes both decisions at the continuation boundary. Claude Code runs [`post-compact-reminder.sh`](../dot_claude/hooks/executable_post-compact-reminder.sh.tmpl) and Codex runs the managed [`compaction-reminder`](../dot_codex/managed-hooks/executable_compaction-reminder.tmpl) as `SessionStart` hooks for the `compact` source; Codex picks up the hook only after the [requirements script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-codex-requirements.sh.tmpl) runs. Codex can [lose the queued reminder if its process exits between compaction and the next turn](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/56316); the managed hook cannot recover that context on resume. [Pi's context extension](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/extensions/compaction-reminder.ts.tmpl) places the text after retained pre-compaction messages and before new messages in each request's context.

## Snowflake CLI execution

Every agent runs the installed Homebrew `snow` through [`~/.local/bin/snow`](../dot_local/bin/executable_snow), a Python script run by Homebrew snow's own interpreter that makes the connector's token-cache factory choose its Linux file cache, `~/.cache/snowflake/credential_cache_v1.json`. One browser sign-in then serves every later `snow` process until the token expires. The cost is the connector's Linux one: until then the token sits in a file that any process running as the user can read, so agents treat that file as a credential store and do not read it. The alternatives cost more: the Keychain asks for approval again in every concurrent process after each Homebrew Python upgrade, and turning the cache off opens a browser sign-in for every invocation.

The wrapper works only while it shadows Homebrew's `snow` on PATH. [Shell startup](#shell-startup) keeps `~/.local/bin` ahead of `/opt/homebrew/bin` in every zsh; wherever Homebrew's `snow` wins, sign-ins and Keychain prompts return. Connector 5 caches through its Rust core and has no such factory, so the wrapper fails at import once an upgrade brings it in, and the token store has to be chosen again.

The wrapper opens the sign-in page through macOS's background opener. On Claude, `permissions.allow` and `sandbox.excludedCommands` run a direct `snow` call outside the sandbox, so that opener works. On Codex, the profile's `~/.ssh` read deny holds every command, `snow` included, in the inner sandbox. There `snow` still writes the token cache through the profile's `:root` write but cannot launch a browser, so Codex's `SNOWFLAKE_AUTH_FORCE_SERVER=true` keeps the connector's loopback callback waiting while the personal `snow` skill opens the printed URL through browser control, which needs an identity-provider session in that browser. Snowflake RBAC owns server authorization. Do not narrow the route to `snow sql -q` or restore workspace `uvx` runtimes.

## Managed skill registry

[`dot_agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`](../dot_agents/skills/) is the canonical source layout for chezmoi-managed skills and is mirrored into `~/.agents/skills`; Claude Code reads that mirror through the managed `~/.claude/skills` symlink, so never add a skill under `~/.claude/skills` directly. Resolve an installed path with `chezmoi source-path` and edit the source, not the deployed copy. Exclude unmanaged installed skills from bulk maintenance, change one only when the user names it, adopt one only when explicitly requested, and leave `~/.agents/.skill-lock.json` as runtime-owned install state. Supporting `references`, `scripts`, and `assets` stay inside their owning skill; the registry has no index, manifest, or category directories.

A skill adopted from a third-party source records under `metadata` the upstream tag it was last compared with and upstream's tree at that tag; adopt only the changes the CLI behavior actually requires, and treat that upstream text as a release-matched reference for current syntax, not permission to overwrite this repository's routing, authorization, or recovery policy. Keep adopted skills out of [GitHub CLI's writing updates](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_skill_update) and [GitLab CLI's skill updates](https://docs.gitlab.com/cli/skills/update/); port changes into source deliberately. A GitHub-hosted skill also records its tag as `github-pinned` to protect that workflow.

The unattended-upgrades job upgrades a CLI silently, so [every `chezmoi apply`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_after_check-skill-versions.sh.tmpl) reports a skill whose recorded tag differs from the installed version of the same-named Homebrew formula. Compare the recorded tree with the skill directory's upstream tree at the installed tag. When it changed, port upstream's diff between the two tags; either way, move the recorded tag, pin, and tree to the installed tag so the report clears. For a GitHub-hosted skill without a same-named formula, check on demand with `gh skill update <name> --all --unpin --dry-run --dir dot_agents/skills`, keeping the upstream command in its documented read-only mode.

The registry deliberately does not:

- Sync an adopted skill by update, merge, or overwrite; a person ports each change.
- Prove that a skill matches its CLI: upstream's skill tree is the only signal, so a behavior change or new capability upstream leaves out of its skill goes unreported, possibly with no failing call ever exposing it.
- Report between applies or hold a CLI back: the unattended-upgrades job only logs, so a CLI can run ahead of its skill until the next `chezmoi apply`.
- Track a skill whose CLI is not a same-named Homebrew formula, or a release Homebrew has not installed; the `orc` skill has [its own report](#rex-integration).

In Claude Code's `auto` mode, a skill's `allowed-tools` skips classifier review during that skill's turn for the concrete non-interpreter CLI prefixes and tools its contract owns, while cross-turn or standing host grants live in `~/.claude/settings.json` (see [`.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md)) and open-ended or interpreter commands stay on the sandbox and classifier path. If Claude denies a matching skill grant, preserve the contract and add the narrowest effective runtime exception backed by a reproducer.

## Identity and encrypted data

[`.chezmoi.toml.tmpl`](../.chezmoi.toml.tmpl) defines prompts for account-specific template values. Each user supplies their own values during `init`; a fork should first review which fields still apply.

Encrypted files use GPG, with private keys stored on a YubiKey. Repository-only encrypted data can seed envchain namespaces in the macOS Keychain instead of deploying credentials as ordinary dotfiles. Adapting the full repository therefore requires replacing or removing its GPG recipients and personal encrypted data.

Agents may read the top-level `~/.ssh` client config (`config`, `config.*`), public keys, `allowed_signers`, and `known_hosts` files, and nothing else under that directory. The [agent guard](#agent-guard) and Claude's sandbox enforce that list by directory, so private keys deployed there need no naming convention and no per-key rule. The Codex sandbox reopens only the exact files ssh and Git signature verification need, so public keys stay unreadable inside that sandbox.

### Git identity and signing

Both forges verify commits signed by the YubiKey, in different formats. GitHub verifies OpenPGP signatures from the card's signature key. GitLab verifies SSH signatures from the card's authentication key against that key as registered on the GitLab account, so the work address never becomes a user ID on the personal OpenPGP key: nothing about the employer is published with that key or has to be revoked from it later. Local Git verifies those signatures against the encrypted `~/.ssh/allowed_signers` instead, which GitLab never reads. [`run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl`](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-gitconfig.sh.tmpl) reads the key id from `gpg --card-status` and installs [`github.config`](../.chezmoitemplates/git/github.config) with it and [`gitlab.config`](../.chezmoitemplates/git/gitlab.config) with the exported authentication key in Git's `key::` form into `~/.config/git/`, so signing reads no file under `~/.ssh`; `dot_config/git/config.tmpl` includes the GitHub file everywhere and the GitLab file for repositories under `~/Code/GitLab/`. The script derives the key itself on every rerun because the GPG script reruns on a Homebrew keg change rather than a card change. Neither script reruns when a YubiKey holding a different key replaces the card, so after such a swap schedule both, `setup-gpg-agent.sh` to import the new card's public key and `setup-gitconfig.sh` to rewrite the signing keys, as [Bootstrap](#bootstrap) describes.

[`git-ssh-gpg-agent`](../dot_config/git/executable_git-ssh-gpg-agent) exists because gpg-agent serves the card's SSH key on `~/.gnupg/S.gpg-agent.ssh` while shells keep the macOS ssh-agent in `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`. The wrapper points `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` at the gpg-agent socket, then runs `ssh` for `core.sshCommand --transport` or `ssh-keygen` as `gpg.ssh.program`, so SSH signing reaches the YubiKey from any shell, including sandboxed agent shells that inherit no agent environment. Git over SSH does too, except in Claude Code's macOS sandbox, which lets no SSH connection out: it sets `GIT_SSH_COMMAND`, which overrides `core.sshCommand`, to a proxy command that cannot authenticate to its proxy. `dot_config/git/config.tmpl` therefore rewrites both forges' `git@` remotes to HTTPS for fetches and pushes alike, authenticated through `gh` and `glab`, so pushing, and fetching a non-public repository, fails while that forge's CLI is signed out. Keeping pushes on SSH would protect nothing while those CLIs' tokens can write to both forges from inside the sandboxes. Bare `ssh` keeps the macOS agent and file keys, except on `github.com` and `gitlab.*` hosts, where `IdentityAgent` names the gpg-agent socket so the card's authentication key is reachable without Git. Changing that socket means updating that entry, the wrapper, and [the shared sandbox Unix socket list](../.chezmoitemplates/sandbox/allowed-unix-sockets.json).

### Credential-backed features

The [seeding script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_seed-envchain.sh.tmpl) reads `.secrets/seed.asc` and stores each entry in the macOS Keychain through envchain. Its plaintext is TOML with one top-level table per namespace and one environment variable per single-line string value; numeric and boolean-looking values remain quoted. The template below is the machine-checked contract for entries consumed by files in this repository; other seed entries are not repository requirements.

```toml
[claude-gateway]
ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN = "replace-with-value"
ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_BASE_URL = "replace-with-value"
ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID = "replace-with-value"
CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_VERTEX_AUTH = "1"
CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX = "1"

[context7]
CONTEXT7_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"

[glab]
GITLAB_CLIENT_ID = "replace-with-value"

[pi]
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"
RC_GATEWAY_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"

[typesafe]
TYPESAFE_API_KEY = "replace-with-value"
```

Each namespace's consumers:

- `claude-gateway`: The [Claude launcher](../dot_local/share/claude-launcher/bin/executable_claude) injects the `claude-gateway` namespace only in gateway mode and otherwise unsets every variable the contract above declares for it, whatever set them, so a `claude` started inside a gateway session follows the persisted mode unless its own flag says otherwise. It is an executable on `PATH` ahead of the native install in `~/.local/bin`, rather than a shell function, so the persisted mode also applies when Pi's bash, a wrapper such as `timeout`, or a script's subprocess runs `claude`.
- `context7`: Every Context7 consumer goes through the [Context7 skill](../dot_agents/skills/context7/SKILL.md), which runs the `ctx7` CLI in `envchain context7` so `CONTEXT7_API_KEY` reaches only the CLI child process. The namespace may also carry an optional `CONTEXT7_BASE_URL`, absent by default; point it, with no trailing slash, at a trusted reverse proxy that forwards the official `/api/v2` query API, and add that host to Claude Code's [sandbox `allowedDomains`](../.claude/rules/claude-code-settings.md#sandbox). The global `--base-url` reaches query-mode requests, but upstream supports custom deployments only for MCP HTTP setup and treats on-premise query mode as unsupported. Validate a Context7 change by running a resolve-and-query through the skill.
- `glab`: The [glab setup script](../.chezmoiscripts/run_onchange_after_setup-glab.sh.tmpl) copies `GITLAB_CLIENT_ID`, the private GitLab's OAuth application ID under the variable name glab itself reads, from the `glab` namespace into glab's configuration.
- `pi` and `typesafe`: The [Pi model configuration](../private_dot_pi/private_agent/private_models.json.tmpl) reads `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `RC_GATEWAY_API_KEY` from the `pi` namespace and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` from the `typesafe` namespace. The [Jev skill](../dot_agents/skills/jev/SKILL.md) runs user-approved local TypeSafe experiments through `envchain typesafe`.

The [agent instruction contract test](tests/agent-instructions.test.ts) parses the TOML block and checks that each key is named by a consumer its entry above links and that each linked consumer names one of the entry's keys, without reading the encrypted seed.
